passage.title: Working from Home: One Year On
passage.text: When Thu's company told staff they could work from home permanently, she was delighted. No more ninety-minute commutes through Hanoi's traffic, and no more expensive lunches near the office. For the first few months, she felt more productive than ever. By the end of the year, however, things had changed. 'I realised I was working longer hours because there was no clear end to the day,' she explains. 'My laptop was always on the kitchen table, so I kept checking emails at ten o'clock at night.' She also missed chatting with colleagues, which she had always found useful for solving problems quickly. Now Thu has found a balance. She goes into the office twice a week and has turned a corner of her bedroom into a small workspace. 'When I close the door, work is finished,' she says. 'It sounds simple, but it has made a huge difference.'

passage.title: The Plastic-Free Café
passage.text: Three years ago, Marco Rossi opened a small café in Bristol with an unusual rule: nothing made of plastic is allowed. Customers who want a takeaway coffee must bring their own cup or borrow one of the café's metal cups, which they return on their next visit. Milk is delivered in glass bottles from a local farm, and food is wrapped in paper or beeswax cloth. At first, some people complained that the system was inconvenient, and Marco admits that his costs are about fifteen per cent higher than those of a normal café. Nevertheless, the business has been a success. 'People like knowing that their morning coffee isn't adding to the rubbish problem,' he says. Several other cafés in the city have now asked Marco for advice, and he has started running free workshops on Sunday afternoons to explain how small businesses can reduce their waste.

passage.title: Can Apps Teach You a Language?
passage.text: Millions of people now try to learn a new language using apps on their phones. The apps are cheap or free, and they make learning feel like a game, with points, levels and daily reminders. Research suggests that they can be very good for building vocabulary and keeping learners motivated. However, many teachers believe apps alone are not enough. 'You can learn hundreds of words, but if you never have a real conversation, you won't feel confident when you travel,' says Dr Helen Park, who teaches at a language school in Seoul. She recommends that learners combine apps with speaking practice, for example by joining a conversation club or finding an online language partner. Another problem is that many users give up after a few weeks. Experts say the secret is to set a realistic goal, such as ten minutes a day, rather than trying to study for an hour and quickly losing interest.

passage.title: A Gap Year in Peru
passage.text: After finishing secondary school, Lucy Grant decided not to go straight to university. Instead, she spent a year travelling in South America, mainly in Peru. For the first four months, she worked as a volunteer at a primary school in a small mountain village, where she taught English and helped the children with art projects. 'The village didn't have reliable electricity, so I had to plan lessons that didn't need computers,' she remembers. 'It made me much more creative.' Afterwards, she travelled around the country by bus, visiting ancient ruins and staying with local families. Lucy admits that there were difficult moments. She was often homesick during the first few weeks, and she once lost her passport, which took ten days to replace. However, she has no regrets. 'I came back more independent and with a much clearer idea of what I wanted to study,' she says. She is now in her second year of a teaching degree.

passage.title: Why Sleep Matters
passage.text: Scientists have known for a long time that sleep is important, but recent studies show just how much it affects our health. Adults who regularly sleep less than six hours a night are more likely to catch colds, put on weight and have problems with concentration. Lack of sleep also affects our mood, making us more easily annoyed and less patient with others. One reason many people don't get enough rest is the light from screens. Phones and tablets give off blue light, which tells the brain that it is still daytime and makes it harder to fall asleep. Experts recommend switching off devices at least an hour before bed and keeping the bedroom cool, dark and quiet. Surprisingly, they also suggest getting up at the same time every day, even at weekends, because a regular routine helps the body clock work properly.

passage.title: Review: Street Food Tour by Motorbike
passage.text: If you only have one evening in Ho Chi Minh City, I strongly recommend booking a street food tour by motorbike. Our guide, Phuong, picked us up from our hotel at six o'clock and immediately gave us helmets and a short safety talk. Over the next four hours, we visited six different places, from a busy market stall serving broken rice with grilled pork to a tiny family restaurant famous for its crab soup. Phuong explained the history of each dish and taught us useful phrases for ordering food. The portions were small, which was sensible, as we would never have managed six full meals! My only criticism is that the tour felt a little rushed at the end, and we didn't have time to try the dessert place on the list. At around $45 per person, including all food and drinks, it was excellent value. Vegetarian options are available if you ask when booking.

passage.title: Should Teenagers Have Part-time Jobs?
passage.text: Should teenagers have part-time jobs while they are still at school? Supporters say that working a few hours a week teaches young people responsibility and the value of money. A Saturday job in a shop or café can also help them develop skills such as communication and time management, which will be useful in their future careers. On the other hand, some teachers worry that jobs take time away from studying. A survey of 2,000 secondary school students found that those who worked more than fifteen hours a week got lower exam results than those who didn't work at all. passage.title: The Science of Happiness
passage.text: What makes people happy? Many of us believe that more money or a bigger house would improve our lives. However, research suggests that once our basic needs are met, extra money makes surprisingly little difference. One famous study followed a group of people for more than seventy years. Those who had close friends and supportive families were happier and even lived longer. Other studies show that spending money on experiences, such as a trip or a concert, brings more lasting happiness than buying objects. This may be because we share experiences with others and enjoy remembering them. Psychologists also recommend simple habits, like writing down three good things that happened each day, which can help us notice positive moments we might otherwise forget.

passage.title: My Grandmother's Kitchen
passage.text: Some of my happiest childhood memories are of my grandmother's kitchen in Hue. Every summer holiday, my parents sent me to stay with her for a month. She would wake me up at five o'clock to go to the market, where she seemed to know every seller by name. She never used a shopping list; instead, she decided what to cook by looking at what was fresh that day. Back home, she let me help, although at first my jobs were limited to washing vegetables and peeling garlic. Gradually, she trusted me with more, and by the age of twelve I could make her famous spicy beef noodle soup on my own. She never wrote her recipes down, so when she passed away last year, I worried they would be lost. That's why I've started a blog where I record every dish I remember, along with the stories she told me while we cooked.

She would wake me up at five o'clock to go to the market, where she seemed to know every seller by name. She never used a shopping list; instead, she decided what to cook by looking at what was fresh that day. Back home, she let me help, although at first my jobs were limited to washing vegetables and peeling garlic. Gradually, she trusted me with more, and by the age of twelve I could make her famous spicy beef noodle soup on my own. She never wrote her recipes down, so when she passed away last year, I worried they would be lost. That's why I've started a blog where I record every dish I remember, along with the stories she told me while we cooked.

passage.title: Is Social Media Making Us Lonely?
passage.text: Social media was designed to connect people, so it may seem strange to suggest that it could make us feel lonely. Yet several studies have found a link between heavy use of social media and feelings of loneliness, especially among young adults. One explanation is comparison: when we scroll through photos of friends at parties or on holiday, we may feel that everyone else's life is more exciting than ours. Another is that time spent online can replace face-to-face contact, which is generally more satisfying. However, researchers stress that it depends on how we use these platforms. Actively messaging friends and arranging to meet seems to have a positive effect, while passively scrolling for hours does not. In one experiment, students who limited their use to thirty minutes a day for three weeks reported feeling less lonely and less anxious than a group who continued as normal.

items.explanation: '…it may seem strange to suggest that it could make us feel lonely.'

passage.title: A Museum With No Walls
passage.text: The National Art Gallery has launched a virtual museum that allows anyone with an internet connection to explore its collection from home. Using a computer or phone, visitors can 'walk' through twelve rooms, zoom in on paintings in extraordinary detail and listen to short audio guides in five languages. The project took two years to complete and involved photographing more than 3,000 works of art. Since it opened in March, the website has had over half a million visitors, many of them from countries where people may never have the chance to travel to the gallery. The director, Ana Lopes, says the virtual museum is not meant to replace real visits. 'Nothing compares with standing in front of an original painting,' she explains. 'But we hope the website will inspire people, especially young people, to come and see the real thing.' In fact, visits to the actual gallery have risen by eight per cent since the website was launched.

passage.title: The Day I Got Lost in Tokyo
passage.text: On my first trip to Tokyo, I decided to explore the city without a guidebook. My phone's battery was full, and I was confident that its map would get me anywhere. By mid-afternoon, however, the battery had died, and I found myself in a quiet neighbourhood with no idea where I was. None of the street signs I could see were in English, and I couldn't remember the name of my hotel's station. I started to panic. Then I noticed an elderly man watering plants outside a small shop. Using gestures and the few Japanese words I knew, I tried to explain my problem. He listened patiently, disappeared inside and came back with a paper map. Not only did he show me the way, but he also walked with me for fifteen minutes to the nearest station. I've never forgotten his kindness, and now I always carry a power bank and write my hotel's address on a piece of paper.

items.question: Why didn't the writer take a guidebook?
options: He thought his phone would be enough.
He had been to Tokyo before.
items.explanation: '…I was confident that its map would get me anywhere.'

passage.title: Food Waste Starts at Home
passage.text: It is estimated that around a third of all food produced in the world is wasted, and a large part of this waste happens in our homes. Families often buy more than they need, cook too much, or forget about food at the back of the fridge until it goes off. Fortunately, there are simple ways to reduce waste. Planning meals for the week and writing a shopping list stops us buying things on impulse. Understanding date labels also helps: 'use by' dates are about safety, but 'best before' dates are about quality, so food is often perfectly safe to eat after its 'best before' date. Leftovers can be frozen or turned into new dishes, such as fried rice or soup. Some apps even allow neighbours to share food they won't use. Reducing food waste not only helps the environment, but can also save an average family hundreds of dollars a year.

passage.title: Advice Column: Choosing a Course
passage.text:
Dear Alex, I'm finishing school next year and I can't decide what to study at university. My parents want me to do medicine because it's a secure career, but I'm much more interested in graphic design. I'm worried that if I choose design, I won't find a good job. What should I do? – Kim

Dear Kim, This is a very common dilemma. First, remember that you will spend at least three or four years studying this subject, so it's important to enjoy it. Students who are passionate about their course usually work harder and achieve better results. That said, your parents' concerns are understandable. Why not research the job market for designers? You may discover there are more opportunities than you think, especially in digital media. It would also be a good idea to talk to people working in both fields. Finally, have an honest conversation with your parents and show them that you've thought about your future carefully. – Alex

passage.title: The Island That Banned Cars
passage.text: On the small island of Saria, there are no cars at all. Visitors arrive by ferry and leave their vehicles on the mainland. Around the island, people get around on foot, by bicycle or in electric carts, which are used mainly to deliver goods and carry elderly residents. The ban was introduced in the 1990s after residents voted to protect the island's peaceful atmosphere and clean air. At first, some business owners were against the idea, fearing that tourists would stay away. In fact, the opposite happened. Saria became famous as a car-free destination, and tourism increased by forty per cent within five years. Today, the island has strict rules to protect its character: buildings cannot be more than three floors high, and new hotels must use solar energy. Locals admit that life without cars can be inconvenient, especially when it rains, but very few would want to change it.

Around the island, people get around on foot, by bicycle or in electric carts, which are used mainly to deliver goods and carry elderly residents. The ban was introduced in the 1990s after residents voted to protect the island's peaceful atmosphere and clean air. At first, some business owners were against the idea, fearing that tourists would stay away. In fact, the opposite happened. Saria became famous as a car-free destination, and tourism increased by forty per cent within five years. Today, the island has strict rules to protect its character: buildings cannot be more than three floors high, and new hotels must use solar energy. Locals admit that life without cars can be inconvenient, especially when it rains, but very few would want to change it.

items.question: Buildings on Saria cannot be more than ___ floors high.
items.explanation: '…buildings cannot be more than three floors high.'

passage.title: Robots in the Classroom?
passage.text: Could robots one day replace teachers? Some technology companies certainly think artificial intelligence will transform education. AI programs can already mark simple tests instantly, adapt exercises to each student's level and answer questions at any time of day. Supporters argue that this could give teachers more time to focus on creative activities and on students who need extra help. However, most educators doubt that machines could do the whole job. Teaching, they point out, is not only about passing on information. Good teachers notice when a student is upset, encourage shy learners and help young people develop social skills. A recent survey of parents found that while seventy per cent were happy for AI to be used as a learning tool, only five per cent would want their children to be taught mainly by a computer. It seems likely that the classroom of the future will combine human teachers and technology, rather than choosing one over the other.
